subject: science
title: KS3 / Year 7-9 Science — Chemistry Basics
subtitle: Reading practice on KS3 chemistry basics, evidence, safety and practical skills.
description: Reading passages for KS3 chemistry basics. Students practise retrieving facts, making inferences and explaining scientific significance from short curriculum-aligned passages.

data.sourcePassage: Chemistry is the study of substances, their properties, and how they change. A substance is a type of matter with particular properties, such as water, oxygen, iron or salt. Chemists investigate what substances are like, how they behave, how they can be separated, and how they react with other substances. Chemistry matters because substances are everywhere: in air, food, medicines, fuels, plastics, paints and cleaning products. In school chemistry, students learn to describe changes carefully and use evidence instead of guesses.

questions.question: Which definition best describes chemistry?
questions.modelAnswer: Chemistry is the study of substances, their properties, and how they change.
options: The study of substances and how they change
The study of planets and stars
The study of maps and rivers

questions.question: Name two examples of substances from the passage.
questions.modelAnswer: Examples include water, oxygen, iron and salt.

questions.question: Why does chemistry matter in everyday life?
questions.modelAnswer: Chemistry matters because substances are everywhere, including in air, food, medicines, fuels, plastics and cleaning products.

questions.question: What scientific habit does school chemistry help students develop?
questions.modelAnswer: It helps students describe changes carefully and use evidence instead of guesses.

questions.question: Which item is a material rather than a complete object?
questions.modelAnswer: Glass is a material because it is what an object can be made from.

data.sourcePassage: A physical change alters the form, state, shape or position of a substance but does not make a new substance. Melting ice, freezing water, dissolving sugar and cutting paper are physical changes. A chemical change makes new substances. The starting substances are reactants and the new substances are products. Burning paper, rusting iron, cooking an egg and magnesium burning in oxygen are chemical changes. Reversibility can be a useful clue, but it is not a perfect test because cutting paper is hard to reverse but still physical.

questions.question: Which example is a physical change?
questions.modelAnswer: Ice melting is a physical change because no new substance is made.

questions.question: What are the starting substances in a chemical reaction called?
questions.modelAnswer: The starting substances are called reactants.

questions.question: What are the new substances made in a reaction called?
questions.modelAnswer: The new substances are called products.

questions.question: Why is cutting paper not a chemical change, even though it is hard to reverse?
questions.modelAnswer: Cutting paper changes the shape and size but does not make a new substance.

questions.question: Explain why reversibility is only a clue, not a rule, for classifying changes.
questions.modelAnswer: Some physical changes are hard to reverse exactly, and some chemical changes may be partly reversed by advanced methods, so the key question is whether a new substance formed.

data.sourcePassage: The particle model explains solids, liquids and gases. In a solid, particles are close together in fixed positions and vibrate. In a liquid, particles are close together but can move around each other. In a gas, particles are far apart and move quickly in all directions. During melting, freezing, evaporation, boiling and condensation, the particles do not become new particles. They change arrangement or movement, but the substance remains the same. Evaporation happens at the surface below boiling point, while boiling happens throughout the liquid at its boiling point.

questions.question: How do particles behave in a solid?
questions.modelAnswer: Solid particles vibrate in fixed positions.
options: They are far apart and still
They move freely in all directions

questions.question: Which change of state is gas cooling to form liquid?
questions.modelAnswer: Condensation is gas cooling and changing into a liquid.

questions.question: Why are changes of state usually physical changes?
questions.modelAnswer: They do not make new particles or a new substance; only the arrangement and movement of particles changes.

questions.question: How is evaporation different from boiling?
questions.modelAnswer: Evaporation happens at the surface and can happen below boiling point; boiling happens throughout the liquid at its boiling point.

questions.question: Why does mass stay the same when ice melts in a sealed container?
questions.modelAnswer: The particles are not lost from the closed system, so the total mass is conserved.

data.sourcePassage: Scientists use observations to decide whether a chemical reaction may have happened. Useful clues include bubbles, colour change, temperature change, light, a new smell, or a solid forming from two liquids. No single clue is perfect by itself. Boiling makes bubbles during a physical change, and mixing dyes can cause a colour change without proving a reaction. A strong conclusion compares observations before, during and after the change and asks whether a new substance has formed. An inference is an explanation based on observations, not the observation itself.

questions.question: Which observation may suggest that a gas has formed?
questions.modelAnswer: Bubbles may suggest that a gas has formed.

questions.question: Give two clues that may suggest a chemical reaction.
questions.modelAnswer: Clues include bubbles, colour change, temperature change, light, smell or a new solid forming.

questions.question: Why is bubbling alone not proof of a chemical reaction?
questions.modelAnswer: Boiling also produces bubbles, but boiling is a physical change.

questions.question: What is the difference between an observation and an inference?
questions.modelAnswer: An observation is noticed or measured directly; an inference is an explanation based on evidence.

questions.question: What makes a conclusion about a reaction stronger?
questions.modelAnswer: A stronger conclusion uses several observations, compares before and after, considers alternative explanations, and explains whether new substances formed.

data.sourcePassage: Laboratory safety protects eyes, skin, lungs, hair, clothing and everyone in the room. A hazard is something that could cause harm. A risk is the chance of harm happening and how serious it could be. A control measure reduces the risk. Students should wear goggles when instructed, tie back long hair, point test tubes away from people, keep bags under benches, and report spills or broken glass. Good practical work also uses suitable equipment. A measuring cylinder measures volume more accurately than a beaker, a thermometer measures temperature, and a balance measures mass.

questions.question: Which equipment measures liquid volume most accurately from the options?
questions.modelAnswer: A measuring cylinder is designed to measure liquid volume accurately.

questions.question: What is a hazard?
questions.modelAnswer: A hazard is something that could cause harm.

questions.question: Explain the difference between a hazard and a risk.
questions.modelAnswer: A hazard could cause harm; a risk is the chance of that harm happening and how serious it could be.

questions.question: Give two control measures for heating a test tube safely.
questions.modelAnswer: Wear goggles, stand up, point the test tube away from people, use a holder and heat gently.

questions.question: Why is choosing suitable equipment part of good science?
questions.modelAnswer: Suitable equipment improves safety and measurement quality, so results are more accurate, precise and trustworthy.
